area: Area VI. Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain and fly a traffic pattern at a towered or nontowered airport to ±100 feet and ±10 knots while talking, and teach a learner to choose the runway and pattern, enter, space and leave it safely, correct for wind on every leg, and handle the first solo pattern.
why: Patterns exist because an airplane cannot stop to give way the way a car can, so a predictable flow is what keeps arrivals and departures apart [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]. Nearly all midair collisions happen at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]], and a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the midairs in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Your learner must be trained in airport traffic patterns, entries and departures before solo [[60:272|14 CFR 61.87(d)(6)]], so the habits you build here fly alone with them.

warmup: Think first: your pre-solo learner flies tidy patterns at the home field, always to the same runway, always with you calling out traffic. Today the wind favors the other runway, the frequency is busy and a glider is being towed. Which of those three changes will show you whether the learner really understands the pattern, and what will you watch for before you say a word?

key_terms.def: The traffic flow prescribed for aircraft landing at, taxiing on, or taking off from an airport [[60:16|14 CFR 1.1]].
The altitude flown in the pattern: the Chart Supplement figure if one is published, otherwise 1,000 feet AGL for propeller airplanes [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]].
The path straight ahead along the extended centerline after takeoff, to at least 1/2 mile beyond the departure end and within 300 feet of TPA [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c1]].

In the AIM, the extension of the departure leg along the centerline that ATC uses for spacing and sequencing [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c2]]. AC 90-66C calls it a path parallel to the landing runway in the landing direction [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]].
A path parallel to the landing runway, opposite to the landing direction [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c4]], flown about 1/2 to 1 mile out [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
A path at right angles to the runway off its approach end, from downwind to the extended centerline [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c5]].
Common Traffic Advisory Frequency: the frequency for airport advisory practice at an airport without an operating tower. It may be a UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS or tower frequency [[1:336|PHAK 14-2]].
Broadcasting your call sign, position, altitude and intentions on the CTAF, used mostly where there is no operating tower or FSS [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.8]].
A ground indicator system at some nontowered airports that can hold the wind indicator, landing direction indicator, landing strip indicators and traffic pattern indicators [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b]].
Landing without entering the pattern. The FAA discourages it for VFR traffic because of midair risk, and it gives no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].
Landing, or trying to land, on the wrong runway, a taxiway or the wrong airport [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other. A skidding one is most likely in a poorly flown base-to-final turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: The pattern, the legs and the standard you hold

body.p: A traffic pattern is the flow prescribed for aircraft landing at, taxiing on, or taking off from an airport [[60:16|14 CFR 1.1]]. Its direction, altitude, entry and exit can depend on local conditions, and the Chart Supplement has the details for each airport [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]. A pilot who knows the basic rectangular pattern can arrive and depart properly at almost any airport, towered or not [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

check.q: The evaluator asks why you teach the AIM leg drawing but warn the learner not to use it for entries. What do you say?
check.a: The AIM note says Figure 4-3-1 only shows the names of the parts of a pattern and should not be used as a guide for entering one [[33:238|AIM FIG 4-3-1]]. Entries come from the key to Figure 4-3-2 and AC 90-66C.

chunks.title: Towered and nontowered: rule or recommendation?

body.p: At a nontowered airport, or one whose tower is closed, the controller's watch is gone from the safety picture and the pilots take over that role [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5]]. The pilot must find the pattern direction, follow the rules and show courtesy, and keep scanning even when traffic seems light [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

head: Item
Rule or recommendation
Source
rows: Powered fixed-wing aircraft approaching to land without an operating tower in Class G turn left, unless approved light signals or visual markings show right turns
Regulation
Same requirements around an airport in Class E airspace
Regulation
Two-way radio with an operating tower, established before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL
Regulation
At a tower: circle to the left unless told otherwise, and get a clearance before landing
Required (AIM restates it)
45° entry at midfield, crossing midfield 500 feet above TPA from the upwind side, 1,000-foot TPA
Recommended practice

body.p: The key line: the FAA regulates traffic pattern flow, not traffic pattern entry [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]]. An aircraft in the pattern counts as approaching to land, so the turn rule applies to it. An aircraft outside the pattern, such as one crossing midfield above pattern altitude to enter, is not bound by 91.126(b) at that point [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]].

Towered airports: the tower can tell you to enter at any point or fly straight in, and jets often fly wider or higher patterns [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]. Not every towered airport has Class D airspace; without weather reporting the controlled airspace normally starts at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, and you still talk to the tower [[33:237|AIM 4-3-2a]]. A suggested heading or direction from a tower with radar is an advisory aid, not a radar vector, and the pilot alone stays responsible for seeing and avoiding other aircraft [[33:239|AIM 4-3-2d]]. Controllers can expect shallow S-turns, but never make a 360 in the pattern without first advising the controller, unless asked to or in an emergency [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]].

Part-time towers: when the tower is closed and no FSS is open, self-announce on the published CTAF inside 10 miles [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.8]]. The 91.126 flow rules keep applying in Class E and Class D airspace, which matters most when a towered airport is operating as a nontowered one [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]].

callout.text: Nontowered airports generally do not require two-way radios, so be especially watchful: a quiet CTAF is not an empty pattern [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]].

Application: have the learner sort every pattern item into 'rule' or 'recommendation' and name the source. Learners who think the 45° entry is law freeze when traffic blocks it; learners who think left traffic is optional fly the wrong way around.

check.q: Your learner asks whether the 45° entry to downwind is required by 14 CFR. What is the accurate answer?
check.a: No. The FAA regulates the flow (direction of turns), not the entry [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]]. The 45° entry at midfield is the recommended method [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]].

chunks.title: Choosing the runway and the pattern for today

body.p: Use the runway most nearly aligned into the wind. A pilot who chooses a secondary runway, for example for length, should stay out of the flow to the into-wind runway [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]]. If other traffic is already in the pattern, use the same runway they use [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].

With a tower, ATC assigns the runway most nearly aligned with the wind when it is 5 knots or more, or the calm-wind runway below 5 knots, unless another runway is operationally better or a runway use program is in effect [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6b1]]. If you need a different runway, advise ATC [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6c]].

No tower and no one talking: check the wind and landing direction indicators from above pattern altitude, then fly to a point well clear of the pattern before descending to enter at TPA [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]]. Check the indicators from well above the pattern in case other aircraft are in it [[24:166|AFH 8-2]].

bullets: Wind direction indicator: the large end of a wind cone or sock points into the wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b2]]. A sock also lets you estimate speed and gusts [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

Landing direction indicator: the small end of a tetrahedron points in the landing direction. Use it for nothing else, and use extreme caution in light or calm wind, when it may not line up with the calm-wind runway [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b3]].

Traffic pattern indicators: L-shaped pairs that show the direction of turns when it is not the normal left pattern [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b5]]. The short member of the L shows the turn direction for the runway parallel to the long member [[24:166|AFH 8-2]].
Mentally enlarge the indicator for your runway and the base and final legs appear; do the same at the departure end for the turn after takeoff [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4c]].

body.p: Pattern altitude: fly the TPA published in the Chart Supplement. Otherwise use 1,000 feet AGL for propeller airplanes and at least 1,500 feet AGL, or 500 feet above the established TPA, for large and turbine-powered airplanes. Cloud clearance under 91.155 may require a different altitude [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]]. Propeller TPAs at most airports run from 600 to as high as 1,500 feet AGL, so look it up every time [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. You may vary the size of the pattern to suit the airplane's performance [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3b]].

Direction: left is standard. Right patterns are set where obstacles, terrain or noise-sensitive areas require them [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.1]]. Sectionals show right traffic as 'RP' with the runways; '*RP' means special conditions, see the Chart Supplement; right patterns are not charted at airports with full-time towers [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3d]].

Today's wind also shapes the legs. With a strong wind on final, or flaps set for a steep descent, put the base leg closer to the runway than normal [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. On downwind, a tailwind means you should not descend too much before base [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

check.q: Over a quiet nontowered field the wind is nearly calm. The tetrahedron points to one runway; the sock hangs limp. How do you teach the learner to use the tetrahedron?
check.a: Only as a landing direction indicator, and with extreme caution in light or calm wind, because it may not be aligned with the calm-wind runway [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b3]]. Cross-check with any traffic seen or heard.

body.p: Wind shear systems (LLWAS, TDWR, WSP, ITWS) show controllers hazardous wind shear and microburst activity near the airport, and controllers relay it to pilots [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]]. More on this in the wind shear chunk.

Teach the information habit as workload management. The learner reviews the chart and sets frequencies early, listens to ATIS, ASOS or AWOS, then monitors the tower or CTAF to picture the traffic, and runs checklists early so there is time for traffic [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. En route, ask the learner to explain the pattern entry and landing preparation they plan [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

callout.text: Application: before every arrival, the learner says five items aloud: runway, direction of turns, TPA in MSL, the entry, and what the wind will do on each leg. If one is missing, the briefing is not done.

check.q: A UNICOM operator tells your learner 'runway 36 is in use.' The sock shows a strong wind from the south. What do you teach?
check.a: UNICOM is not required to give information and has no standards for it [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.3]]. Check the wind indicators even when CTAF information is given, because there is no assurance it is accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. Use the runway most nearly into the wind, or the one other traffic is using [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]] [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].

chunks.title: Entering, flying and leaving the pattern

body.p: Nontowered patterns are always entered at pattern altitude [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Know the TPA before you arrive and stay clear of the flow until you are on the entry leg [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

head: Arriving from
Method
rows: The downwind side
Fly 45° to the downwind leg toward a point abeam the runway midpoint, and join at midfield [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Make the entry leg long enough to see the whole pattern and plan [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
The upwind side (preferred)

Announce, cross midfield at least 500 feet above TPA (normally 1,500 feet AGL), or at 2,000 feet AGL if large or turbine aircraft use the airport. About 2 miles clear, scan, descend to TPA, then turn right to enter on the 45° at midfield [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
The upwind side (alternate)
Midfield crosswind at TPA, scan, announce, then turn downwind. Do not use it when the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Give way to aircraft on the 45° and on downwind [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]

body.p: Why the 45° is preferred: a pilot who meets conflicting traffic on it can keep turning away from downwind, fly a safe distance away and come back for another try, scanning all the while [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Before joining downwind, adjust course or speed to fit the traffic [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

bullets: Downwind: about 1/2 to 1 mile out at TPA; finish the before-landing checks and lower retractable gear [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

Hold TPA until at least abeam the approach end, then reduce power and start down [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. Turn base at about 45° relative bearing from the approach end [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.4]] with a medium bank [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
Before turning final, make sure no one is already close on final [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Finish the turn to final at least 1/4 mile from the runway [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]].

After takeoff or a go-around, continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end, watching for pattern traffic [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]]. On a go-around, once safe, make a shallow turn to the upwind side to see departing traffic [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
Staying in the pattern: turn crosswind beyond the departure end within 300 feet of TPA [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]], and turn downwind at TPA [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].
Leaving: straight out, or a 45° turn in the pattern direction, beyond the departure end after reaching TPA, after checking for traffic entering [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.8]].

body.p: Speeds come from the POH/AFM [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.9]]; on downwind they generally fall between 70 and 90 knots for typical piston singles [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. The PHAK splits that into 70 to 80 knots for fixed-gear singles and 80 to 90 for high-performance retractables [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]]. Always adjust to fit the other traffic [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]. Extend flaps in steps on downwind, base and final so pitch and power changes stay small, and retrim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

callout.text: Level, 45, midfield. Every entry ends the same way: at TPA, on a 45° to downwind, joining abeam the middle of the runway [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.3]].

check.q: Your learner, arriving from the upwind side, crosses midfield at TPA because 'it's faster,' while two airplanes are on downwind. What do you point out?
check.a: The midfield crosswind entry at TPA is only the alternate method and should not be used when the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]]. Use the preferred method: cross 500 feet above TPA, fly about 2 miles clear, descend and enter on the 45°.

body.p: Right-of-way rules apply all through the pattern [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]]. The general rule: when weather permits, every pilot keeps watch to see and avoid, IFR or VFR, and a pilot who must give way may not pass over, under or ahead of the other aircraft unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

head: Situation
Who has the right-of-way
rows: Distress
The aircraft in distress, over all other traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]
Converging, same category, about the same altitude
The aircraft on the other's right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
Converging, different categories

Balloon over all; glider over powered aircraft; airship over powered aircraft except one towing or refueling; an aircraft towing or refueling over all other powered aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
Head-on
Each pilot alters course to the right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(e)]]
Overtaking
The aircraft being overtaken; the overtaking pilot alters course to the right and passes well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]
On final or landing
Over aircraft in flight or on the surface, but may not force off an aircraft that has landed and is clearing the runway [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]
Two aircraft approaching to land
The lower one, but it may not use the rule to cut in front of or overtake an aircraft on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]

bullets: Gliders, including the tow aircraft while towing, have the right-of-way over powered aircraft. Where airplanes and gliders share a runway, the glider pattern is inside the powered pattern [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]] [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.2]].
Ultralight vehicles must yield to all aircraft [[17:17|AC 90-66C 12.3.1]]. Remote pilots of drones must always yield to manned aircraft [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.10.1]].
A straight-in pilot, IFR or VFR, has no priority over aircraft in the pattern and must comply with 91.113(g) [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g4]].
Even when you have the right-of-way, yield if another aircraft seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

body.p: Teaching it: the AIH says it is imperative to introduce the 91.113 right-of-way rules to the learner [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Teach 'right-of-way' as 'who must give way,' never as 'who may go.' A learner on base who sees an airplane on final and thinks 'I'm lower, so I have it' needs to hear the second half of 91.113(g) before solo.

check.q: Your learner, on downwind in a trainer, converges at the same altitude with a tow plane pulling a glider that is on the learner's right. The learner says, 'It's on my right, so it has the right-of-way anyway.' Is the reasoning complete?
check.a: The answer is right but the reason is incomplete. An aircraft towing other aircraft has the right-of-way over all other powered aircraft no matter which side it is on [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)(4)]] [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]].

chunks.title: Spacing and situational awareness in the pattern

body.p: At a nontowered airport you are expected to see who is already in the pattern and conform to the pattern in use, entering well clear of them [[24:166|AFH 8-2]]. Fit in before you join downwind by adjusting course or speed, then set power so you are neither too fast nor too slow [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

bullets: Following traffic: keep it in sight and fit in by adjusting course or speed [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. At a tower, a pilot who decides to make maneuvering turns to keep spacing should advise the controller if at all possible [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]].

A conflict on base or final: if the turn to final would create a collision hazard, go around or maneuver to avoid; a pilot rushing the turn to get space has good reason to go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
Traffic on the runway: allow time for it to clear; if a conflict looks likely, go around early [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

Do not announce your own landing sequence, such as 'number 3'; that is ATC's job at towered airports [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]]. Ask other pilots to clarify intentions you do not understand [[17:12|AC 90-66C 10.1]].
Multiple runways: scan for operations on other runways, and at a nontowered airport use the CTAF to ask which runway another aircraft is using [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.5]].

body.p: Situational awareness is the accurate perception of the factors that affect safety, and monitoring radio traffic helps a pilot build a mental picture of what is happening [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. You can test it: ask the learner where the other aircraft in the pattern are. If the learner gives too much attention to one task and loses track of traffic or control, point out that awareness is not being kept [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

callout.text: Application: in a busy pattern, ask 'Who are we following, and where is he now?' at least once each circuit. A learner who can't answer is flying the airplane but not the pattern.

check.q: On base your learner sees that the airplane ahead has not cleared the runway and steepens the turn to 'buy time.' What do you teach?
check.a: If there may be a conflict, an early go-around is in order [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Rushing or tightening the turn to make space is itself a reason to go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

body.p: The pattern is a rectangular course flown around the runway. The rectangular course exists partly to prepare the pilot for the airport traffic pattern [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], so teach the pattern as that maneuver with a runway in it.

body.p: The rule behind it: the higher the groundspeed, the steeper the bank needed for the same track [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

callout.text: The base-to-final overshoot is the classic killer. An unrecognized tailwind on base makes the learner turn late, overshoot the centerline, then add bank, back elevator and inside rudder to swing the nose around. That sets up a skidding cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin. The safest fix for an overshoot is a go-around; at that height be reluctant to bank more than 30° and never skid the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Orientation means always knowing where the runway in use is. At night, fly toward the beacon until the runway lights stand out, positively identify the threshold and edge lights before flying the pattern, and set the heading bug on runway heading as a reference for the legs [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].
With parallel runways, do not overshoot final or fly a track that crosses the final approach or departure path of the other runway [[33:243|AIM FIG 4-3-3]].

On every final, verify the runway number and alignment. Unfamiliar airports, complacency and fatigue lead pilots to line up with the wrong surface while thinking all is normal; study the airport diagram and lighting ahead, and go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

check.q: Your learner's base legs start with a high groundspeed and keep ending past the extended centerline. What wind does that point to, and what do you teach?
check.a: A tailwind component on base, which the AFH names as the setup for a late turn and an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Higher groundspeed needs a steeper bank and an earlier turn [[24:153|AFH 7-7]], with a crab to keep the base track square [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. If it still overshoots, go around rather than tighten the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: The NTSB names pilots failing to see and avoid as the most probable cause of midair collisions [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Using any pattern, service or procedure never reduces the pilot's duty to see and avoid from ramp-out to ramp-in [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

bullets: When and where: mostly in daylight and good visibility, between aircraft going the same direction, at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet, involving pilots of all experience levels, most not on a flight plan [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
Instructors are no guarantee: one study found a flight instructor on board in 37 percent of midairs, and involved pilots ranged from first solo to 20,000-hour veterans [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Blind spots: high wings hide what is above, low wings what is below; the worst case is a low-wing airplane above a high-wing airplane. Bank now and then to uncover blind spots and look behind [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

Descending entries: one aircraft could descend on top of another already in the pattern. All similar aircraft, including those on the 45°, should be at the same altitude so they are easier to see [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]].
Straight-ins: the FAA does not recommend a VFR straight-in when others are in the pattern; it can conflict with aircraft on base and final [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]].

Unusual traffic: no-radio aircraft [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]], 'flight check' aircraft that may fly nonstandard or opposite-direction patterns and low approaches [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.1]], and drones that need no radio and may be hard to see [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.10.1]].

body.p: Mitigations from the AFH list: tune and verify frequencies before the airport area, monitor the CTAF, report 10 miles out and listen, report entering downwind, turning base and turning final at a nontowered airport, descend to TPA before entering, keep a constant visual scan, expect radio-less aircraft, and use exterior lights to be seen [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. Keep lights and strobes on [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.10]].

Teaching it: if learners believe the instructor carries the whole lookout, they never build the habit, so make the learner own the scan from the first lesson, and correct at once any tendency to start a maneuver without clearing [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. During instruction, have the learner verbalize clearing, for example 'clear left, right, above and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Scanning technique itself is taught in Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance; here, tie it to pattern positions.

check.q: Your learner flies a low-wing trainer and is about to turn from downwind to base at a busy field. Which conflict is hidden from both pilots, and what do you teach before every turn?
check.a: A high-wing airplane below and a low-wing airplane above can't see each other; that is the worst case [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Before turning base, bank slightly or look to uncover blind spots and check that no one is already close on final [[24:169|AFH 8-5]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

chunks.title: Risk: distractions, priorities, lost awareness and disorientation

body.p: Congestion, aircraft climbing and descending, and pilots busy with cockpit duties all raise accident risk near the airport, and marginal VFR makes it worse [[33:237|AIM 4-3-1]]. The pattern is short, low and busy, so it is where distraction costs the most.

head: Threat
What the sources say
How you teach against it
rows: Distractions
Most stall/spin accidents happened with the pilot's attention diverted; 60 percent occurred during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Practice planned distractions at altitude first, then hold the learner to coordinated, correct airspeed in every pattern turn
Task prioritization
Plan, prioritize and sequence tasks; when overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]
Checklists done early on downwind or before entry; flying the airplane always comes first
Loss of situational awareness
The first sign of high workload is working harder but accomplishing less; then the pilot fixates on one item [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]
Ask about traffic positions to test awareness [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]; offer the 45° turn-away or a go-around as the way to buy time [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]
Disorientation
Wrong surface landings follow unfamiliarity, complacency or fatigue [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]; at night distance and height are deceptive [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]
Airport diagram study before flight, runway number check on every final, heading bug on runway heading [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]

body.p: Habit can disorient too. The AIH describes a learner assigned runway 30 for many days who, given runway 12, turns to enter the pattern for runway 30 out of habit. That is a slip, and hurrying makes slips more likely [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. Vary runways, airports and entries so the learner has to think about each arrival.

Model the sterile flight deck: the airline rule bans nonessential activity in critical phases, including all ground operations, takeoff and landing, and the AIH says it holds for the whole aviation community and the instructor should model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. In the pattern, that means no teaching chatter on short final either.

callout.text: Application: a good test question while en route is 'What will we do when we get there?' The AIH suggests asking the learner to explain the pattern entry and landing preparation in advance [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. If the plan exists before the airport, the pattern workload drops.

check.q: On downwind your learner fumbles a flap switch, re-reads the checklist twice and does not notice the altimeter is 150 feet low. What is happening and what is the fix?
check.a: Work overload: working harder but accomplishing less, then fixating on one item [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Fly the airplane first, then stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Next time, run the checks earlier so the downwind is free for traffic and altitude [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

chunks.title: Risk: wind shear and wake turbulence

body.p: Wind shear is a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area. Near the ground it is especially dangerous, and it is commonly associated with passing fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and strong upper winds over 25 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A tailwind turning to headwind raises airspeed and performance; a headwind turning to tailwind lowers them [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

A microburst is the most severe type: typically 1 to 2 miles across and about 1,000 feet deep, lasting 5 to 15 minutes, with downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots. Clues can be a heavy rain shaft, virga, or only a ring of blowing dust. On approach, the sequence of headwind, downdraft, then tailwind can force an airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Wind shear may be reported but often goes undetected [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Alerts: LLWAS gives wind shear and gust front information around the airport edge, but not microburst alerts; controllers give the airport wind, then the boundary wind [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7a]].

Wake turbulence: every aircraft makes it, so be ready for it in any pattern, especially in trail of other aircraft, and avoid the area below and behind the generating aircraft, mainly at low altitude [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]]. Strength rises with weight and falls with speed; the strongest wake comes from a heavy, slow, clean airplane, because flaps and gear hasten wake decay [[1:361|PHAK 14-27]].

head: Near the ground
What to teach
rows: Vortex movement
Vortices sink several hundred fpm; within 100 to 200 feet of the ground they move sideways at 2 to 3 knots [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Worst wind
A light quartering tailwind can leave vortices along much of the final approach, not just the touchdown zone [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Landing behind a larger aircraft, same runway
Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Landing behind a larger aircraft departing on the same runway
Note its rotation point and land well before it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b4]]
Landing behind a larger aircraft departing on a crossing runway

Note its rotation point. If it rotated past the intersection, continue and land before the intersection. If it rotated before the intersection, avoid flight below its path, and abandon the approach unless a landing is ensured well before the intersection [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b5]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
After its low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go

Make sure at least 2 minutes have passed before your takeoff or landing; the hazard can lie along the runway and your flight path, particularly in light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]

body.p: Gusty pattern days: many pilots add one-half of the gust factor to the normal approach speed, within the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Teach the learner that an approach the wind has made unstable ends in a go-around: in a pattern, go around at once if the approach becomes unstable below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: A large jet departs on a runway that crosses yours. You see it rotate beyond the intersection as your learner turns final. Where should your learner plan to land?
check.a: Before the intersection. The jet's wake begins at its rotation point [[1:361|PHAK 14-27]], so when it rotates past the intersection, continue and land before the intersection [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b5]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

chunks.title: Reading the airport from the pattern

body.p: The CFI examiner expects you to identify and interpret runways, taxiways, markings, signs and lighting and explain them while flying (ACS AI.VI.B.S1). In the pattern, these are the items that change what the learner does next.

head: What you see
What it means for the pattern
rows: Runway numbers

Magnetic azimuth of the centerline to the nearest 10° [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6a]]; parallel runways add L, C or R [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]], shown left to right as seen from the approach direction [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6a]]
Displaced threshold: white arrows to a 10-foot white bar
Shorter landing length. The area behind it is for takeoff either way and for landing from the opposite direction [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]]
Relocated threshold: 10-foot white bar, yellow arrowheads before it
The closed part is not for takeoff or landing, only taxi, and the opposite runway is shorter too [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]]
Yellow X at each runway end
Runway closed. Some closures have no visual sign, so always check NOTAMs and ATIS [[1:349|PHAK 14-15]]
Segmented circle and L-shaped indicators
Pattern direction for each runway [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b]]
Rotating beacon, white and green
Civilian land airport; sometimes on in daytime below VFR minimums, but there is no requirement for that, so you judge the weather [[1:350|PHAK 14-16]]
VASI or PAPI

Glidepath information, day or night; a VASI gives obstruction clearance within 10° of the extended centerline out to 4 NM [[1:350|PHAK 14-16]]; a PAPI is a single row, normally on the left side [[1:350|PHAK 14-16]]
Red runway holding position sign

The airport version of a stop sign, where a taxiway meets a runway [[1:341|PHAK 14-7]]. At an uncontrolled airport, don't enter the runway safety area without making sure of separation from other aircraft [[1:340|PHAK 14-6]]
Runway safety area boundary sign (yellow, faces the runway)
Leaving the runway, you are out of the safety area once the whole airplane passes the sign and its marking [[1:340|PHAK 14-6]]

body.p: Teaching it: brief the airport diagram on the ground, then ask the learner on downwind to point out the threshold, any displaced threshold, the wind sock and the exit taxiway they plan to use. Correct answers spoken in the air show the learner can read the airport while flying, which is what the pattern demands. (application)

check.q: On downwind your learner sees white arrows leading to a white bar at the approach end. The learner plans to touch down on the arrows to 'use all the runway.' What do you say?
check.a: That is a displaced threshold. The arrowed area may be used for takeoff in either direction and for landing from the opposite direction only, not for landing in your direction [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: from first pattern to first solo

body.p: Build it in blocks. The learner masters segments separately and then combines them, simple to complex [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. For the pattern, that means ground reference work first (the rectangular course prepares the pilot for the pattern [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]), then the pattern at the home field in light wind, then crosswinds, busy traffic, the other runway and other airports. The AIH names pattern congestion, a change in active runway and unexpected crosswinds as challenges the learner masters one at a time before facing them together [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

head: Phase
What you do
rows: On the ground
Draw the pattern for today's runway and wind: TPA in MSL, entry, where the crab goes on each leg, where to descend, go-around plan, and who has the controls
Your demonstration
Fly one complete pattern while explaining each point as you reach it; keep TPA ±100 feet and speed ±10 knots while you talk (ACS AI.VI.B.S5)
Learner flies
Learner talks through each leg as they fly it; you watch eyes, altitude and the ground track, and always guard the controls, ready to take them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Scenario practice

Have the learner plan an arrival to a specific nontowered airport: wind, arrival path, communication procedures, available runways, recommended pattern and what to do if the unexpected happens, then make the decisions in flight with your guidance [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]
Check understanding
If the learner flies it right but may not understand, make them vary it: another runway, the other entry, a different airport [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

body.p: Letting errors run: it is often better, safety permitting, to let a learner go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. In the pattern 'safety permitting' is narrow: a wide downwind or a late descent can run, but a skidding base-to-final turn cannot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Take the controls calmly with 'I have the flight controls' when it can't [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Presolo paperwork is part of the lesson plan: you administer the presolo knowledge test on parts 61 and 91, the solo airport's airspace rules and procedures, and the airplane, then review every incorrect answer before authorizing solo [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]]. The learner must have logged training in airport traffic patterns, entries and departures, and in collision, windshear and wake turbulence avoidance [[60:272|14 CFR 61.87(d)(6)]] [[60:272|14 CFR 61.87(d)(7)]].

Practice landings: speed and control come first. Full-stop landings build control, allow careful checklist use and leave time to teach. Stress touching down in the first third of the runway or going around, and going around after an oscillation or a significant bounce [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

The first solo pattern: the learner must show consistent traffic pattern operation among the solo skills [[25:163|AIH 8-5]], and the decision should be a joint one when the learner performs consistently without your help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. Be present for the first solo; pick a time of day with the traffic, wind, sun angle and reflection in mind; have a portable radio so you can end the solo if something develops, keep radio calls to a minimum, and do not talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Full-stop landings on the first solo give you the chance to stop the flight [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Debrief right after, while the flight is fresh [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: Your learner flies excellent patterns, but only ever to runway 30 at the home field. How does the AIH suggest you find out whether the learner really understands the pattern?
check.a: Make the learner vary the performance, combine it with other operations or apply the same elements elsewhere, such as the other runway or another airport. A learner who doesn't understand the principles usually can't [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: The AFH has no error list in its pattern chapter. This table is built from the cautions in AFH chapter 8, AC 90-66C and the approach and rectangular course error lists [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Descending into the pattern
Learner arrives on the 45° still descending through TPA
Level at TPA before the entry leg; one aircraft can descend onto another [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]] [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Entry leg too short
Joins downwind seconds after starting the 45°, no time to find traffic
Start the 45° far enough out to see the whole pattern [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Straight-in into a busy pattern
Learner wants to 'save time' with traffic on downwind
Fly the pattern; VFR straight-ins are discouraged and get no priority [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]]
Too fast or too slow for the traffic
Closing on traffic ahead or holding up traffic behind
Set power on downwind to fit the flow [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]
Altitude or speed wanders while configuring
Balloons or sinks with each flap change; heavy control pressure
Flaps in steps, retrim after each [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]; checks done early [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]
Descending before abeam the approach end, or too much with a tailwind
Low on base, dragging in with power
Hold TPA until abeam; plan for the tailwind on downwind [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Poor wind assessment and drift correction
Pattern legs drift wide or narrow; no crab on base
Assess wind before entry and set a wind correction angle on each leg [[24:153|AFH 7-7]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]
Overshooting final, then skidding the turn
Steep bank with inside rudder and nose dropping toward the runway
Go around; don't exceed about 30° of bank or skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]
Stretching the glide with elevator
Nose comes up, airspeed decays, sink increases
Add power with pitch; elevator alone leads to a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Raising flaps to fix an undershoot
Sudden sink close to the ground
Add power and pitch instead [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Pressing on with an unstable approach
Still correcting big errors below 300 feet AGL
Go around at once if unstable below 300 feet AGL in a pattern [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Lining up on the wrong surface
Aimed at a taxiway or the parallel runway
Check runway number and alignment on every final; go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Flying the habitual pattern
Turns toward the usual runway's pattern after a runway change
Brief the new runway aloud; vary runways in training [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]

callout.text: When you analyze an error for the examiner, name it, say what you saw, give the cause and give one fix. 'Late base turn, wind from behind on downwind pushed us long, fix: turn base earlier and steeper' beats a list of five corrections.

check.q: Your learner, low on final, raises the nose without adding power and the vertical speed increases. Which listed error is this, and what is the fix?
check.a: Trying to reach the runway with elevator alone [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Add power along with the pitch change; pitch alone raises the angle of attack, bleeds airspeed and can lead to a high sink rate or low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

scenario.title: First solo day at a busy nontowered field
scenario.setup: It is Saturday afternoon at a nontowered airport in Class G with runways 9-27 and 18-36, a published TPA of 1,000 feet AGL and left traffic on all runways. The AWOS gives wind 230 at 6. Your pre-solo learner has flown three good dual patterns today. A tow plane is launching gliders from runway 27, a business jet has just made a low approach to 27, and the CTAF is busy. You plan to step out for the learner's first supervised solo, three full-stop landings.

questions.q: Which runway should the learner use, and why?
questions.a: Runway 27. It is the runway most nearly aligned into the wind (270 is 40° from 230; 180 is 50° away) [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]], and it is the runway the other traffic is already using [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]].

questions.q: Before you get out, what does the AIH say about timing and your setup for a first solo?
questions.a: Be present to help; consider the time of day for traffic congestion, wind, sun angle and reflection; have a portable radio if possible so you can end the solo if a situation develops [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. A busy Saturday afternoon may argue for waiting.

questions.q: The learner's pattern converges with the tow plane and glider. Who has the right-of-way, and where does the glider pattern usually sit?
questions.a: The glider and the tow plane while towing have the right-of-way over powered aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]] [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]]. On a shared runway the glider pattern is inside the powered pattern [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.2]].

questions.q: The jet's low approach to runway 27 was made in a light quartering wind. What is the wake plan before the learner takes off or lands?
questions.a: Make sure at least 2 minutes have passed since the larger aircraft's low approach, because vortices settle and move sideways near the ground and can lie along the runway and the flight path, particularly in light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

questions.q: On the second solo circuit, the learner extends downwind behind a slow airplane, and you see a faster one entering on the 45°. What do you say on your radio, and when?
questions.a: Keep radio calls to a minimum and use the radio to stop the solo only if a situation is developing; never talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. The learner was trained to adjust course and speed to fit the traffic [[24:169|AFH 8-5]], so let the plan work unless safety requires you to speak.

questions.q: After the third full stop, what happens next?
questions.a: Debrief immediately while the flight is vivid, and answer every question the learner has [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Full-stop landings were required so you could stop the flight at any time if needed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

skills.do: Point out and explain runways, taxiways, markings, signs and lighting from the pattern and on the ground: runway numbers, displaced or relocated thresholds, closed runway X, segmented circle, beacon and VASI/PAPI.
skills.practice: On every flight, name each item aloud from downwind and say what it changes [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]] [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]].

skills.do: Fly the recommended entry, legs and departure (45° entry level at TPA, base turn at about 45° relative bearing from the approach end, final completed at least 1/4 mile out, crosswind within 300 feet of TPA) while explaining each point.
skills.practice: Script your patter against the key to AIM FIG 4-3-2 and fly it at two different airports [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

skills.do: Hold a square ground track with crab angles on each leg and the right bank in each turn for the groundspeed, and explain why.
skills.practice: Fly patterns on a crosswind day and call the crab on each leg and the bank in each turn aloud [[24:152|AFH 7-6]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

skills.do: Keep and explain orientation to the runway in use: identify the runway early, use the heading bug as a leg reference, verify the runway number on final.
skills.practice: Set the heading bug on runway heading every pattern; say the runway number on every final [[24:227|AFH 11-10]] [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Maintain traffic pattern altitude, ±100 feet, and the appropriate airspeed, ±10 knots, while explaining (ACS AI.VI.B.S5).
skills.practice: Fly patterns from the right seat while talking without stopping; have a friend note the worst altitude and speed deviation on each leg [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

skills.do: Show situational awareness and spacing: find and call each pattern aircraft, fit in by course and speed, extend or go around when needed, and explain the choice.
skills.practice: At a busy field, call out who you follow each circuit and say your spacing plan [[24:169|AFH 8-5]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct the examiner's simulated pattern errors: name the error, what you saw, the cause and one fix.
skills.practice: Drill the error table: for each error, practice the one-sentence diagnosis and fix [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: A pilot crosses over midfield 500 feet above pattern altitude to set up a 45° entry. According to AC 90-66C, is that pilot bound by the 91.126(b) left-turn rule at that moment?
options: Yes, every aircraft within 4 NM of the airport is bound by it at all times
No, an aircraft outside the traffic pattern is not bound by 91.126(b)
Only if the airport has a segmented circle showing left traffic
Only in Class E airspace
quiz.why: AC 90-66C notes that an aircraft outside the pattern, such as one crossing midfield above pattern altitude to enter, is not bound by 91.126(b) [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]].

quiz.q: A tower controller tells your learner, 'Proceed southwestbound, enter a right downwind runway three zero.' What is that instruction, in AIM terms?
options: A radar vector the learner must fly exactly until the tower says otherwise
A clearance to land
An advisory aid; the pilot keeps sole responsibility to see and avoid
A request the learner may ignore without telling the tower
quiz.why: Generalized directions and suggested headings from a tower radar are advisory aids to VFR pilots, not radar vectors, and the pilot alone stays responsible for seeing and avoiding [[33:239|AIM 4-3-2d]].

quiz.q: At a part-time towered airport after the tower closes, where might the learner find the automated weather?
options: Only by calling the FSS on the phone before departure
Nowhere; automated weather goes off the air whenever the tower closes for the night
On the ground control frequency, which stays on as a recording
On the ATIS frequency, which some such airports use while the tower is closed
quiz.why: Some part-time towered airports broadcast the automated weather on their ATIS frequency during the hours the tower is closed [[33:274|AIM 4-3-27b]].

quiz.q: What downwind airspeeds does the PHAK give for typical piston singles in the traffic pattern?
options: About 70 to 80 knots fixed-gear, 80 to 90 knots for high-performance retractables
About 100 to 110 knots for all singles, to keep up with faster traffic
The final approach speed, set on downwind so nothing changes later
VY for every airplane, so a go-around needs no change of attitude
quiz.why: Pattern speeds generally fall between 70 and 80 knots for fixed-gear singles and 80 to 90 knots for high-performance retractables, and the manufacturer's recommended speeds should be used [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]]; adjust the speed to fit the other traffic [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

quiz.q: Your learner checks the sectional for 'RP' at an airport with a full-time control tower and finds nothing. What does the AIM say?
options: No 'RP' means every runway there uses left traffic, with no exceptions
Right traffic patterns are not shown at airports with full-time towers
The sectional is out of date, so the flight should be postponed
Full-time towers never use right traffic, so the question cannot come up
quiz.why: Sectionals show right patterns as 'RP' with the runway numbers, but right traffic patterns are not shown at airports with full-time control towers [[33:240|AIM 4-3-3d]]; the tower and the Chart Supplement give the direction.

quiz.q: Where does the AFH say a skidding cross-control stall is most likely?
options: During a steep turn at altitude, when the load factor is at its highest
On downwind abeam the numbers, as power comes off for descent
On the takeoff roll, when the nose is raised too early
In a poorly planned base-to-final turn, often after an overshoot
quiz.why: A skidding cross-control stall is most likely in the pattern during a poorly planned and executed base-to-final turn, often with an unrecognized tailwind on base [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: Which ordinary pattern challenges does the AIH say a learner should master one at a time before facing them together?
options: Engine failure, radio failure and smoke in the cabin, practiced together early
Night flying, instrument conditions and mountain flying at high density altitude
Traffic pattern congestion, a change in active runway and unexpected crosswinds
Short, soft and obstacle fields
quiz.why: The AIH lists pattern congestion, a change in active runway and unexpected crosswinds as ordinary challenges the learner masters individually before performing them collectively [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

quiz.q: Behind a relocated threshold, the closed part of the runway may be used for:
options: Taxi only
Takeoff only
Landing in either direction
Nothing at all
quiz.why: With a relocated threshold, the closed part is not available for takeoff or landing but is available for taxi [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]].

quiz.q: Your learner says wake turbulence only matters behind jets. What does AC 90-66C say?
options: Correct; light aircraft make too little wake to matter, even to another trainer
Wake only matters at towered airports
All aircraft make wake; avoid the area below and behind them, especially low
Wake is only a cruise-altitude problem
quiz.why: All aircraft generate wake turbulence, so expect it in the pattern and avoid the area below and behind the generating aircraft, especially at low altitude [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what does the NTSB name as the most probable cause of midair collisions?
options: Radio failures that keep pilots from announcing their positions
Pilots failing to see and avoid other aircraft
Nonstandard pattern entries flown at the wrong altitude
Faster airplanes overtaking slower ones on final approach
quiz.why: According to the NTSB, the most probable cause of midair collisions is the pilot failing to see and avoid other aircraft [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

final_quiz.q: The tower at your training field closes at 2100. At 2130 your night learner asks which way to fly the pattern and how to report. What do you teach?
options: Any direction is fine with the tower closed, as long as she announces her direction on the CTAF
Fly right traffic, because night patterns are reversed at part-time towered fields
Call the closed tower anyway on the tower frequency and wait for an answer
Fly the 91.126 flow, left unless marked, and self-announce on the CTAF within 10 miles
final_quiz.why: With the tower closed and no FSS, self-announce on the published CTAF within 10 miles [[17:7|AC 90-66C 9.8]]. The 91.126 flow rules continue to apply, especially when a towered airport is operating as nontowered [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Arriving at an unfamiliar nontowered field, your learner plans a 1,000-foot AGL pattern without looking anything up. What does the PHAK say about propeller pattern altitudes?
options: They are always exactly 1,000 feet AGL, so there is nothing to look up
Any altitude is fine as long as it is announced on the CTAF first
They are always 1,500 feet AGL at nontowered fields, the same as for jets
They generally run from 600 to as high as 1,500 feet AGL, so look each one up
final_quiz.why: Traffic pattern altitudes for propeller-driven aircraft generally extend from 600 feet to as high as 1,500 feet AGL [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]; fly the published TPA, or 1,000 feet AGL if none is published [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]].

final_quiz.q: During supervised solo practice, a learner's pattern looks unsafe as a jet calls 5 miles out. What does the AIH say about your portable radio?
options: Talk the learner through every leg so the solo stays safe and the jet stays clear
Never use it during a solo flight, since any call breaks the learner's concentration
Use it to end the solo if a situation develops, keep calls few, and never talk on short final
Use it to tell the jet to go around or extend, since the solo learner has priority
final_quiz.why: A radio lets the instructor terminate the solo if a situation develops; keep communications minimal and never talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Night arrival at an unfamiliar field: your learner can see the beacon but can't yet pick out the runway, and wants to enter downwind on a guess. What does the AFH say?
options: Fly toward the beacon until the runway lights stand out, and identify threshold and edge lights first
Enter downwind on the beacon's side, since the beacon always sits beside the runway
Descend to pattern altitude early so the runway lights are easier to see
Circle the beacon at pattern altitude until the tower calls with a runway
final_quiz.why: At night a pilot should normally fly toward the rotating beacon until the runway lights are distinguishable; the threshold and runway-edge lights must be positively identified to fly a pattern of proper size and direction, and a heading bug set to runway heading helps [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

final_quiz.q: With a strong wind on downwind, your learner descends early and arrives low on a long base. What do the sources tell you to teach for next time?
options: Fly the same pattern every time and just add full power on final to drag it in
Turn base later and farther out, so the strong headwind on final has more time to slow the airplane
Don't descend too much on a tailwind downwind, and put base closer when the final wind is strong
Descend well before abeam the approach end, so the tailwind can't carry her long
final_quiz.why: Pilots should consider tailwinds and not descend too much on downwind [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. With a strong wind on final, position the base leg closer to the approach end [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

final_quiz.q: A broken layer sits low enough that your learner can't fly the published 1,000-foot AGL pattern and keep cloud clearance. What does AIM 4-3-3a allow?
options: Flying a different altitude when the 91.155 distance-from-cloud criteria require it
Nothing; the published TPA must be flown even if that means flying in the clouds
Flying the pattern 500 feet higher, above the broken layer, to keep the clouds below
Only straight-in approaches
final_quiz.why: The recommended pattern altitudes should be held unless another TPA is published or unless the 91.155 distance-from-cloud criteria require otherwise [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3a]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner, flying at an unfamiliar airport in the evening, says the runway 'looks a bit narrow' on final and keeps going. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Continue, since the GPS map shows the airport ahead and the runway will come into view
Slip to lose altitude and land
Turn on the landing light and continue
Verify alignment and runway number, and go around if in doubt about the surface
final_quiz.why: On every final, verify runway alignment and number; unfamiliarity and fatigue lead to wrong surface landings, and if there is doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner descends through TPA on the 45° entry 'to be configured early.' Why does AC 90-66C object?
options: It wastes fuel and leaves the airplane low and slow too far from the runway on downwind
It confuses the AWOS
It violates 91.126(b), which makes the 45° entry and its altitude a regulation
One aircraft could descend on top of another already in the pattern, and similar aircraft at one altitude are easier to see
final_quiz.why: Descending into the pattern can put one aircraft on top of another; all similar aircraft, including those on the 45°, should be at the same pattern altitude so they are easier to acquire visually [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]].

final_quiz.q: Wind favors runway 27, and two airplanes are in its pattern, but 27 is short and wet today. Your learner wants the longer runway 18 for landing distance. What does AC 90-66C say about using a secondary runway?
options: She may, but should stay out of the flow to the runway most aligned into the wind
Use any runway freely; at a nontowered field the first pilot to call sets the runway
A secondary runway may be used only after the into-wind pattern is empty for 10 minutes
She must use 27 like the others in every case, even if it is too short for her
final_quiz.why: Use the runway most nearly aligned into the wind; a pilot who uses a secondary runway, for example for length, should avoid the flow of traffic to the into-wind runway [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's friend rides along and chats through the pattern, and you join in. What does the AIH say about this?
options: Fine on a VFR training flight
The sterile flight deck idea holds for all pilots, and you should model it
Only Part 121 airline crews must avoid it, so it does not apply to training
Allowed if the learner is ahead of the airplane
final_quiz.why: The sterile flight deck rule came from airline accidents but holds true for the entire aviation community, and the instructor should teach and model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner, used to runway 30 for weeks, is told to use runway 12 and starts toward the runway 30 pattern. How does the AIH classify this, and what makes it more likely?
options: A mistake from a misconception; fatigue makes it more likely
Willful noncompliance; overconfidence
A slip from habit; time pressure makes slips more likely
A knowledge gap; poor ground school
final_quiz.why: The AIH gives this exact example of a slip from doing a routine task in a slightly different way, and notes that hurrying produces more slips [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].

final_quiz.q: No one is on the CTAF at a nontowered field. Your learner descends to pattern altitude 3 miles out, then overflies the field at TPA to read the wind sock. What does AC 90-66C recommend instead?
options: Overfly at TPA as planned, since the sock is easier to read from low down
Check the indicators from above pattern altitude, then go well clear and descend to enter at TPA
Skip the sock and land on the longest runway, since the field is empty
Fly a low pass down the runway at 500 feet AGL to look at the surface and the sock
final_quiz.why: Determine the wind and runway in use from the indicators while at an altitude above the traffic pattern, or from other traffic's calls; then proceed to a point well clear of the pattern before descending to and entering at pattern altitude [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]].

final_quiz.q: At a nontowered field with two runways, your learner can't see the far runway's threshold during the run-up. Another pilot calls 'departing' without a runway. What do the sources recommend?
options: Assume they use the same runway as you and take off right behind them
Ask on the CTAF which runway the other aircraft is using
Taxi onto the runway to look down its length for the other airplane
Wait for UNICOM to sequence both departures on the frequency
final_quiz.why: Where line of sight to other runways is poor, at a nontowered airport use the CTAF to ask other departing aircraft which runway they are using [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.5]]. Don't enter the runway until no conflict exists [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5.1]].

takeaways: The FAA regulates pattern flow (turn direction, tower contact), not entry; the 45° entry, midfield crossing and 1,000-foot TPA are recommendations [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]].
Enter level at TPA; the 45° is preferred because you can turn away and come back [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].
Right-of-way means who must give way; the lower aircraft may not cut in front of one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].
Teach the pattern as a rectangular course with a runway: crab on each leg, steeper bank where groundspeed is high [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
An overshoot on final means go around, never a skidding turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Make the learner own the lookout and the plan; ask where the traffic is [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].
First solo: be there, pick the time, keep the radio quiet, full stops, debrief at once [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
cfi_notes: Leg names differ by source. The AIM defines the upwind leg as a path that begins after departure and continues straight ahead along the extended centerline, used by ATC for spacing and sequencing, and says its terms are the standard for towers and pilots [[33:238|AIM 4-3-2c2]]. AC 90-66C Appendix A defines it as a path parallel to the landing runway in the landing direction, separate from the departure leg [[17:19|AC 90-66C App A]], and AFH 8-4 also calls it a course parallel to the landing runway, flown at towered airports and after go-arounds [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Teach the AIM terms, and show the learner the other meaning so a call of 'upwind' is understood either way.

Crosswind turn wording: AC 90-66C 11.7 says not to start the crosswind turn until beyond the departure end and within 300 feet below pattern altitude, and to turn downwind at pattern altitude [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]]. The AIM key says within 300 feet of pattern altitude [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]], and so does AFH 8-4 [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. For a climbing airplane it is the same point (700 feet AGL under a 1,000-foot pattern). AC 90-66C adds that the crosswind leg may be longer or shorter in unusually hot or cold weather [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].

Pattern speeds: the AFH gives 70 to 90 knots for typical piston singles [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]; the PHAK gives 70 to 80 for fixed-gear and 80 to 90 for high-performance retractables [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]]. They agree; the POH/AFM governs [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.9]].

The AFH pattern chapter has no common-error list. Build your error patter from the rectangular course list (AFH 7-7) and the approach and landing list (AFH 9-10), and say so if the examiner asks where it comes from.

The cross-control stall is a demonstration maneuver that only CFI applicants may be asked to perform [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Tie it to the base-to-final turn in your pattern lesson so the learner sees why you insist on coordinated turns and a go-around for any overshoot.

Don't let 'letting the learner find the mistake' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] reach the base-to-final turn. Decide on the ground which pattern errors you will let run (wide downwind, late descent) and which you will stop at once (skidding turn, slow airspeed low).

The AIH asks you to consider the time of day for a first solo [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; at a busy training airport that often means early morning or a weekday. The sources give no traffic limit; that judgment is yours.

This lesson leaves radio phraseology to the Communications Task (AI.VI.A) and scan mechanics to Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance (AI.II.B). In the pattern lesson, focus on position reports as a tool for spacing and awareness [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

Wake rules differ slightly by source. PHAK 14-28 says to land 'prior to' a departing aircraft's rotation point and to wait 2 minutes, worst in a quartering tailwind [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]; AIM 7-4-6 says land 'well prior to' the rotation point and applies the 2-minute interval particularly in light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Teach the AIM wording.
gaps: Pattern speeds, flap and gear schedules and power settings are airplane-specific; use the POH/AFM. The sources give only generic figures (70 to 90 knots on downwind, 1.4 VSO on base, 1.3 VSO on final).
The sources give no step-by-step wind shear escape technique for light single-engine airplanes; the PHAK points to AC 00-54, which is not in the resources [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Airport-specific TPAs, right traffic remarks, noise abatement and part-time tower hours are in the Chart Supplement, which is not in the resources.
No source sets traffic, wind or time-of-day limits for a first solo; the AIH leaves it to the instructor's judgment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
Seaplane base patterns in the Task title are not taught; this lesson covers single-engine land airplanes only.

activities.title: What the learner says, what you teach
activities.intro: Match each learner statement to the correction the sources support.

pairs.l: 'The 45° entry is required by the regulations.'
pairs.r: The FAA regulates pattern flow, not entry.

pairs.l: 'I'm lower, so I can turn base in front of him.'
pairs.r: The lower aircraft may not cut in front of one on final.

pairs.l: 'Tower gave me a heading, so they're watching traffic for me.'
pairs.r: Suggested headings are advisory; see and avoid stays with you.
UNICOM has no standards; check the wind indicators.
It shows landing direction only, and is unreliable in calm wind.

pairs.r: VFR straight-ins are discouraged and get no priority.

activities.title: Pattern numbers
activities.intro: Work each number from the rules in the lesson, then type your answer.

items.q: Field elevation 1,280 feet MSL, no published TPA, propeller airplane. Pattern altitude in MSL?
Same field. On the CFI checkride, what is the lowest altimeter reading on downwind that still meets the standard?
Same field, arriving from the upwind side by the preferred method, with turbine aircraft using the airport. Midfield crossing altitude in MSL?
items.why: With large or turbine aircraft, stay at 2,000 feet AGL: 1,280 + 2,000 = 3,280 feet MSL [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

items.q: TPA is 1,000 feet AGL and the learner stays in the pattern. Lowest height AGL to start the crosswind turn?
items.why: Within 300 feet of TPA: 1,000 - 300 = 700 feet AGL, and beyond the departure end [[33:241|AIM FIG 4-3-2]].

items.q: The trainer's VSO is 52 knots. Target airspeed on base using the AFH rule?
Same airplane, no manufacturer's recommendation. Final approach speed?

activities.title: True or false: who else is out there
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Recreational drones generally need no authorization in Class G and need not talk on the radio.
cards.why: True. Drones generally need no authorization in Class G and are not required to keep radio contact; they must yield to manned aircraft [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.10.1]].

cards.s: A 'flight check' aircraft may fly a nonstandard or opposite-direction pattern.
cards.why: True. Flight inspection aircraft may fly nonstandard or opposite-direction patterns and low approaches [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.1]].

cards.s: Landing gear and flaps down make a heavy airplane's wake stronger.
cards.why: False. A 'dirty' configuration hastens wake decay; the strongest wake is heavy, clean and slow [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]].

cards.s: Where airplanes and gliders use the same runway, the glider traffic pattern is inside the powered-aircraft pattern.
cards.why: True [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.2]]. Watch inside your pattern turns as well as outside.

cards.s: Most pilots involved in midair collisions were on a flight plan.
cards.why: False. The majority were not on a flight plan [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

cards.s: Ultralight pilots should fly a pattern 500 feet below and inside the standard pattern.
cards.why: True. AC 90-66C puts the ultralight pattern 500 feet below and inside the standard pattern for the airport [[17:17|AC 90-66C 12.3.2]].

activities.title: A busy Saturday dual lesson
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner is flying you to a nontowered airport with runways 18-36 and 9-27. The AWOS gives wind 200 at 8, and two airplanes report left downwind for runway 18. You arrive from the west, the side opposite the runway 18 downwind.

steps.s: Ten miles out, the learner wants a straight-in to runway 27 because it is closer. What do you teach?
options: Go ahead, announce it and land
Land on 27 but fly a left pattern for it
Use runway 18 like the traffic already there, and fly the pattern
Circle overhead until the others land
steps.why: If traffic is in the pattern, use their runway [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11]]; 18 is also more nearly into a 200 wind [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]]. VFR straight-ins are discouraged [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

steps.s: Arriving from the upwind side, the pattern busy. How do you enter?
options: Cross midfield at least 500 feet above TPA, fly about 2 miles clear, descend, then turn onto the 45° to downwind
Cross midfield at pattern altitude, then turn into the crosswind leg ahead of the other traffic
Descend to pattern altitude well before the field, then fly through the pattern to the 45°
Join downwind directly from the crosswind side at TPA + 500, then descend once established on downwind, ahead of the others
steps.why: That is the preferred upwind-side entry; the midfield crosswind alternate is not for a busy pattern [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

steps.s: On the 45°, a Cub is on downwind just ahead and a Bonanza is closing behind. The learner can't see a safe gap. Now what?
options: Squeeze in between the Cub and the Bonanza by slowing and calling your intentions on the radio
Turn away from downwind, fly clear and come back to the 45°, scanning all the way
Do a 360 on the downwind leg to open up room behind the Cub, calling it on the radio
Descend below pattern altitude to pass under the Cub, then climb back up into the pattern after it
steps.why: That is exactly why the 45° is preferred: turn away, fly a safe distance and return [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

steps.s: On the next circuit the learner turns final late, overshoots the final approach course, then adds bank and bottom rudder. What do you say?
options: 'More rudder, bring the nose around faster to get back on the final approach course'
'Go around, then fly another circuit and try the turn again'
'Pull harder and steepen the turn to get back on the course sooner'
'Hold the bank with opposite aileron so the turn does not steepen'
steps.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; a skidding, steepening turn sets up a cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: Later, a King Air ahead makes a touch-and-go in a light quartering wind just as the learner turns base. Plan?
options: Land right behind it, short of its touchdown point, since any wake from its touch-and-go has already moved away
Ignore it; turboprops make no wake, so continue base and land with normal spacing
Fly below its path to stay out of the wake and keep the base turn tight to land soon after
Extend or go around so at least 2 minutes pass after its touch-and-go before you land
steps.why: After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, make sure at least 2 minutes have passed before you take off or land; the hazard can lie along the runway, particularly in light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
